4.	The more important and specific instructions issued in this connection to census commissioners are as follows:-
Appointment of enumerators.-After proper enumeration sub-districts have been established and approved by the Bureau of Statistics it will be your duty to select a suitable person in each sub-district to perform the actual work of enumeration. This is a very important duty and you must exercise the greatest possible care to secure competent persons. Your own success as commissioner and the success and value of the census as a whole are absolutely dependent upon the thoroughness, accuracy and promptness with which the enumerators perform their duties. The Book of Instructions clearly sets forth the duties and qualifications of the enumerators, while the specimen schedules of population and agriculture and the examination papers relating thereto should enable you to select only such persons as have the capacity for efficient service. You are particularly enjoined to reject all applicants who are unable to pass the examination test satisfactorily and in such cases you are authorized to immediately fill the vacancy. It will be a mark of your fitness for the posi-

Questions
tion to which you have been appointed to make yoitr selection in the first instance in such a way that the numbers of those who will be unable to pass the test w-ill be as small as possible.
Residence of enumerators.-To ensure the best results each enumerator appointed should, as far as practicable, be an actual resident of the sub-division within which his duties are to be performed. This ensures familiarity with the territory and the general character of the people residing in the district he is to canvass. Only in cases where a competent resident of an enumeration area cannot be found should a selection be made of a person living elsewhere. An enumerator should be thoroughly familiar with the boundaries of the various units which are contained within the area assigned to him.
Qualifications of enumerators.-The enumerators should be active, energetic persons of good address, as outlined in Section 35 of the Book of Instructions.
The following classes of persons are suggested as likely to make good enumerators, and they are specially recommended to your favourable consideration:-(a) In rural districts, crop correspondents of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics; (b) School teachers when available and able to give their time to the work; (c) Officers and leading workers in farmers' organizations, live stock associations, co-operative creameries, etc.; progressive farmers and their sons and daughters; and especially young men or women who have attended agricultural colleges or agricultural experimental stations.
It is further suggested that, in certain sections, women would make excellent appointments as census enumerators owing to the fact that in many instances the information must be obtained from the female head of the house. In the last census several women acted as enumerators and gave excellent results.
Enumerators must give their entire time to census work.-It is absolutely essential that applicants for the position of enumerator should understand that their whole working time will be required during the period of enumeration. It will be impossible for an enumerator to complete his district in the allotted time if he undertakes to carry on at the same time any work or business.

I would ask the Prime Minister if it is the intention of the government to verify the report of a speech made by Canada's High Commissioner, the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, at Leeds, Yorkshire, as reported by the Canadian Press on April 28. It appears in the Ottawa Journal under the heading of "Ferguson points to U.S. Influence.'' In the body of the report occurs this passage:
What was happening at present was that out of $4,500,000,000 invested in Canada from outside sources, $3,500,000,000 was American capital and barely $1,000,000,000 from this country.
Then follows the paragraph which I wish particularly to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister:
Think of the insidious influence in that connection with its introduction of American executives, American methods and contacts.
I should like to ascertain from the Prime Minister if he thinks this is of sufficient importance to verify the accuracy of the report, and if he finds it is accurate, will some attempt be made to cramp the style of Canada's High Commissioner?

speechtext: I thought I might explain it in committee. I did explain it briefly on the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. I can give the explanation now just as well. In the year 1928 an agreement was come to between the province of Saskatchewan and the Dominion gOYr-ernment under the terms of which police work in the province of Saskatchewan was taken over by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and at the same time certain portions of the provincial police force were incorporated in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. When the agreement was completed and executed on the 22nd of March, 1928-1 may say that the agreement appears in full in the report of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for the year 1928-there was one clause outstanding as to which sufficient data had not then been received to make the document complete. That clause related to the pensions of those men of the provincial police force who were being absorbed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That clause is as follows:
15.	(a) Arrangements will be rvorked out
whereby men taken from the Saskatchewan provincial police under this arrangement and included within the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shall be entitled to the pension benefits now received by members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and such men shall be entitled to credit for all service performed prior to the first of June, 1928, in either the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or the Saskatchewan provincial police, and the government of Saskatchewan shall contribute to the Dominion government such reasonable Sum as shall be necessary towards the Dominion gorr-ernment pension fund to enable such men to get the benefit in computing their pension for the number of years served with the Saskatchewan provincial police.
The names of those entitled to pension have now been definitely settled. They comprise four officers and fifty-five non-commissioned officers and men formerly in the provincial force and now in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force. In respect of these men a subsequent agreement has been made and executed by the authorities of the province of Saskatchewan and by the Department of Justice to provide in accordance with the preliminary agreement for the absorption of these provincial police upon the same terms in regard to pension as is provided in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police pension scheme. The province of Saskatchewan bears its pro rata cost of the expense. This act is merely to authorize the taking over of these men for the purpose of pension.

I did not rise to oppose the bill, but I might point out that my hon. friend spoke of having explained this bill when the resolution was before the house. I would remind him that the bill was not preceded by a resolution, but was read on April 17 for the first time.

The purpose of the bill is to extend to certain men provisions for pension which do not apply to them under the present law. In my view it is certainly in the nature of a money bill.

Personally I feel that during a period of depression more than at any other time public authorities should spend large amounts on public works. It appears on this occasion, however, that this is reversed, and the policy seems to be one of practising economy, which, as I have said before, means that more people will be thrown out of employment. Mr. Chairman, before we
deal with the individual items under this vote I desire for a few moments to refer to a statement which the minister read when the committee met this afternoon. This statement was given in response to my request a few days ago for certain information with regard to the appropriations and expenditures for 1930-31. In looking over the statement, I notice, as the minister said-and this, of course, includes only the Public Works department-that a total of $38,099,727.70 was voted at the general session of 1930, of which only $32,981,613.74 was expended-or a balance unexpended of $5,118,113.96. In answer to the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) the hon. minister sought to set up an alibi by stating that other governments had done the same thing, that is. not expended the full amount of the vote. I am surprised that because previous governments, and especially Liberal governments, had not expended the full amount appropriated that the minister should use that as an excuse for not spending money voted before the Conservative government came into power last August. It is quite true that this money was voted three or four weeks before parliament was dissolved, but the present government had an opportunity in August, September, October and November, of spending this $5,000,000 odd,-or perhaps more, because it is quite likely that some of the $38,000,000 was expended during those months. I say it is a pretty small excuse for the Conservative government and for the Minister of Public Works to give, as a reason why this money was not expended, that the previous administration, in former years, did not spend the money which was voted by this parliament. May I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that there was a different condition existing last year than existed in 1929, in 1928 and in previous years. This country was prosperous during those years and perhaps there was not the necessity for spending public money in this country.

According to the estimates there is a reduction of approximately $1,250,000 in the expenditure on public buildings in Ontario this year. In view of the unemploy-

ment situation in this province, does the minister consider it a good thing to reduce the expenditure on necessary public buildings and at the same time grant employment relief through other channels?

I can only repeat what I have mentioned frequently, that these buildings are constructed out of the revenues, and we are going as far as we think the revenues of Canada warrant in the construction of public buildings at the present time.

I do not think the minister got my point. Last year we voted $20,000,000 to make grants to the provinces and municipalities for unemployment relief. After all is said and done, the revenues come from the taxpayers of Canada, whether they be collected by the municipalities, the provinces or the federal government. My thought is that, we might well have gone on with our building program and spent money in that way through the construction of necessary public buildings. As the minister said, the revenue of the country has to be considered. If however we are going to spend it, would it not be better to spend it on our own public works rather than hand it out to some other body to spend in some other way?

I think my hon. friend will agree that the manner of spending the money is a matter of policy. He has laid down, I believe the principle that the relief of unemployment is primarily a provincial and municipal matter, and that the federal government may properly assist when unemployment becomes acute. Undoubtedly lie will agree with me that funds providing for the relief of unemployment should be fluid and available for expenditure where unemployment exists in the greatest measure. If an item were placed in the estimates the funds would be available for expenditure only on that particular work at that particular place, so that an item in the estimates would not meet an emergency as effectively as a direct vote for the relief of unemployment when from time to time urgent conditions arise. The principle has been adopted of securing knowledge of local conditions through the cooperation of the provinces and municipalities. On reflection I think my hon. friend will agree that the direct vote is better fitted to give a greater measure of relief than is a fixed amount in the estimates for some particular place where unemployment may not be acute. On the other hand it might so happen that such moneys would not be available where conditions were unfavourable. At the time we were discussing in the house the unemployment situation, and the intention of the government of that day in voting the money was to carry on as rapidly as possible the proposed public works to provide employment. The general election takes place, the government of the day is defeated, a new government comes into power, a special session is called in September, and in order to relieve the unemployment situation the Prime Minister states to this house that in addition to the money already voted by parliament it is necessary to vote $20,000,000. It was clearly pointed out to the minister by myself personally, and by various letters that, he received, that the situation existing in that counity was such that the people were practically on the verge of starvation. The necessary expenditure had been authorized by parliament, tenders had been called for, the minister himself recommending that the lowest tender be accepted at a figure of $6,000 less than the cost of the work as estimated by the engineers of the department. After receiving appeal upon appeal the minister's heart was softened, he went to council to recommend
that this work be carried out. I received from the minister the following reply, dated April 24:
Dear Mr. Beaubien:
I have your letter of the 22nd instant, with reference to a post office building in Dominion City, Man.
At the time the matter of awarding the contract was under consideration, a careful review of the financial situation disclosed that the revenues were decreasing, and as buildings of this character are erected out of revenue, it was felt that circumstances at the time did not warrant the government in proceeding with the construction of this building.
As you know, revenues have not increased, and under the circumstances, it is not thought that the public interest would be seriously prejudiced by the erection of this building not being proceeded with. The small revenue from the office, namely about $1,300 would not appear to warrant an expenditure on the construction of a public building at Dominion City at the present time.
It may be true that the revenues from this office are not very large, but the postal business is being carried on in a store and every hon. member knows the inconveneince of a post office being conducted in a general store. It seems to me that the all-important question in regard to the expenditure of public money is that the will of parliament be snpreme. At the last session of the last parliament the then Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) introduced an item of $12,000 for the construction of this public building. The item was placed in the estimates because of the representations which had been made to him with regard to the inconvenience resulting from this post office being in a general store. No other building was available in the town for post office purposes. The estimates were brought down, the item was passed in

committee of the whole, the present Minister of Public Works, then in opposition, as well as other hon. members in opposition, allowing the item to pass. I see no reason why the will of parliament should not take precedence over every other consideration. The Prime Minister in nearly every speech he has made has advocated that our parliamentary institutions be respected and that the will of parliament be supreme. But how can we respect the parliament of Canada if an item passed unanimously by the house, advertised in the newspapers all over the country, is disregarded, the new Minister of Public Works -I do not accuse the hon. minister of any unfairness; far be it from such-claiming as an excuse that the revenues of the country are decreasing and therefore this work should not be gone on with. During the special session of parliament I urged that this building should be constructed. I was told by the minister that the matter was under consideration. When I returned home after prorogation, in answer to telegrams sent to the department I was told that the matter was still under consideration. The representatives of that municipality came to me and asked me when I expected the contract would be let. In a growing and young country such as Saskatchewan many public buildings are needed. I can state that in every constituency in Saskatchewan public buildings are required. Looking through the estimates one thing impressed me more than anything else. I have sat in this house for the last four or five weeks and have heard people talk about a depression existing in this country. The people who talked most about the depression were the farmers from the western prairies, and more particularly from Saskatchewan. There is more talk about unemployment and depression in western Canada than anywhere else. Bearing that in mind I would ask hon. members to look at the estimates for public buildings. We find that moneys are not to be expended where they should be; public buildings are not to be located where they should be located. The Minister of Public Works made a statement in connection with the new immigration hall at North Battle-ford. I am very glad he made that statement. As I watched him when he was making it I felt that he was very anxious to give r.he house that information, and I am very glad the house and the. country have received these details.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that there was a new immigration hall built in North Battle-ford last year. North Battleford is one of the keys to the north country; Prince Albert is

another and Edmonton is still another. There was a new immigration hall built at Edmonton which cost, I believe, about $75,000, while the hall at North Battleford cost between $25,000 and $30,000. The immigration hall at Prince Albert was completed the year before, and cost between $30,000 and $40,000. What do these expenditures mean? These-immigration halls were undertaken largely because of the vision Canada had a few years ago with regard to a greater population. The war had built up a vast national debt, and the feeling had spread throughout the Dominion that we should have a greater population to bear that debt. Consequently not only the Conservative party but the Liberal party of the day felt that immigration was necessary. I am sure my hon. friend will remember the vision of immigration into this country given the house and the country a few years ago by the organizer for his own party, Mr. McRae. His proposition was that each year for ten years we should spend $30,000,000 on immigration, giving a total expenditure of $300,000,000. Can anyone wonder that when the party then in opposition, led by such men as the minister and the organizer of his party, went across Canada advocating greater immigration this vision was accepted and anticipated by these public buildings to accommodate those who were to come to this country?
I might say that personally I think the construction of that building in North Battleford was in order and I believe that every official of the Department of Public Works who knows anything about North Battleford and that north country will admit that fact. With regard to the old building I say to the-minister that it was a disgrace to Canada to-bring any mother or family from any part of the world for the purpose of settling in that north county and leave them overnight or for a week or more in that old building in North Battleford. That being the case certainly I set myself to do all I could to have a new immigration hall erected there, and I succeeded in having that building constructed. I believe the day is coming when, if we do not accept the vast scheme advocated by the Conservative party when in opposition in regard to immigration, at least we will need' a greater population, and we are going to-select that population from the best people outside of Canada. We have stopped immigration for the time being, but we have no proof that this is to be a permanent policy. It is only a temporary expedient, as the minister well knows. Consequently, when the time comes for immigration to flow into this country again that building, which is worth

Mr. Chairman, while
this item is under discussion I should like to discuss another matter in which a rather important principle is involved. Some little time ago I placed a question on the order paper with regard to the redecoration of the interior of the post office at Red Deer. I was informed that two men had tendered for the work, that the lowest tender had been accepted and the work had been completed. I have no exception to take to the man chosen to do the work, because he is a man of probity, a skilled worker, and his charge was a reasonable one. There is no question
[Mr. H. A. Stewart.1
about that. My reason for placing the question on the order paper was this:	In the
little city of Red Deer three or four men carried on that kind of work. One of those men, a man of good standing, came to me and made this complaint. He said that when the tenders were called for, he, together with the two whose names are mentioned in the answer given, offered tenders for consideration and he was informed very definitely that instructions had been issued that no tenders could be accepted for consideration-the minister will appreciate the difference between, "accepted for consideration" and "accepted"- save from two whose names are given in the reply which I received. So this man went back with his tender in his pocket. According to him, his tender was refused all consideration because his name was not on the favoured list, and as supporting the right party. The minister will see, in the first place, that I am not making this statement as something of which I have personal knowledge I do not know first-hand that this man was refused consideration. I am simply passing on to the minister the complaint that was made to me in a very serious, not to say energetic, manner by a man whose probity there was no reason to doubt, a business man of good standing. If he was right in his complaint as to the treatment he received, he complained with very good reason. If that did happen, it is a very serious thing. It is not a matter of small political patronage which we know occasionally happens in the best of families and in the best of parties. But it is a serious matter from the public point of view if a tender which may be the lowest, and may be a satisfactory tender in every other respect, is not considered because of the political views of the would-be tenderer. I cannot expect the minister to know anything about it just nowr; indeed, I doubt if he ever knew anything about it; but I would ask him to look into the matter very closety and ascertain whether the answer given on April 22 to the question I placed on the order paper is the full and complete answer, and to assure himself that neither from anywhere in his department nor from anywhere connected with his department have such instructions or suggestions gone forth; because, as he will readily appreciate, such a matter strikes at the root of the decency and honesty of all public service. In bringing the matter to his attention I am not making any charge. I have watched the minister in the house, and I believe that he is efficient and fair and doing his best to carry on his work. I bring the ir^ter to his

Supply-Public Works-B.C.
attention simply because the complaint was made to me in all seriousness by a business man of good standing, and because I think it should be looked into very carefully. If anything like that was done, steps should be taken to prevent its happening again. I shall be glad to give to the minister the name of the complainant and any other names concerned. He will appreciate, of course, why I am not making the name public at the moment.

I want to thank the hon. member for bringing this matter to my attention. I can assure him that no instructions of that character have been issued by the minister or by any person with his authority, and none will be. I shall certainly investigate the matter.

Item agreed to.
Drumheller-public building-under contract, $60,000.
Is the work on this building progressing satisfactorily, and when will it be completed?

The contract
was awarded on February 2, 1931. The date for completion is September 3, 1931. I should think at this season they will be going right ahead with the work, and we shall endeavour to see that it is completed on time.
The original contractors are carrying on satisfactorily, I take it?

As far as I
know.
Item agreed to.

Before we pass from the
Alberta vote, may I say that some time ago the town of Viking sent a petition to the Minister of Public Works requesting a public building at that point. I notice that no such provision has been made in the estimates, and I would ask the minister just what attention that petition has received.

I can assure my hon. friend that I have many such petitions, and they have been the subject of much serious and anxious consideration by me. I regret that not more of them appear in the estimates. I will look this particular one up and see how it stands.
British Columbia-Dominion public buildings -improvements, repairs, etc., $45,000.

The constituency of Skeena, which I have the honour to represent, includes the city of Prince Rupert.
Prince Rupert has no such thing as a federal public building. The federal government are just renting a shack which a reputable farmer would not use as a barn. We have had it for a number of years. A delegation from the city of Prince Rupert waited upon the government within the last two weeks, and I understand that they were given the assurance that when the present lease pxpires their representations will be given serious consideration. We have in Prince Rupert, which has a population of approximately 10,000, a provincial building which cost about $500,000. Prince Rupert, as some hon. members realize and others do not, occupies a strategic position as- a British Pacific port at the terminus of the Transcontinental railway. I understand that the government gave the representatives from the city of Prince Rupert and the chamber of commerce a good hearing, and no doubt the claims of the city will be given consideration. But when I see only the small amount of $45,000 in the estimates for improvements and repairs to Dominion public buildings in British Columbia, I think it is up to me as a member representing one of the ridings of that province to remonstrate and to say that that is not doing justice to British Columbia. I trust that the government will look into the matter and see that central and northern British Columbia are given consideration in the supplementary estimates. I repeat that because of Prince Rupert's location at the end of a (transcontinental railway and as a. British Pacific port it occupies a strategic position. It stands third in customs and post office revenue in British Columbia. Prince Rupert is the second British North America port on the Pacific, and I am sure hon. members on both sides of the house will agree that we cannot develop British North America as it should be developed unless we do justice to the port of Prince Rupert. From the fact that only $45,000 is appropriated to the province of British Columbia for improvements and repairs to public buildings, one might almost think the government.had forgotten that such a place as British Columbia exists.
Before I sit down I would like to impress my hon. friends opposite with the fact that Prince Rupert lies in a strategic position also in respect to northern and central British Columbia. At the present time we have only this rented shack, which accommodates customs, post office, telegraphs, fisheries, and public works. For that shack we are paying something like $7,000 a year in rent. I received that information from the Minister of Public Works, who wras kind enough to give



Supply-Public Works-B.C.
it to me. I think the government would be saving money if it would consider the erection of an adequate public building in the city of Prince Rupert.

The claims of Prince Rupert have been strongly urged upon the government, and have been supplemented by my hon. friend to-night. Many representations have been made to the department by the people of that city. Let me assure my hon. friend that the claims and requirements of Prince Rupert will not be overlooked, and as soon as revenues warrant it the construction of a building will be considered. I can only ask my hon. friend to be patient. The item of $45,000 is the same amount as that voted last year. It is for general upkeep and repair of public buildings in British Columbia. No new building is included in this item.
Of that amount how much was expended in the last year?
It was all required last year.

I would add that the Dominion government did buy a federal site about ten or twelve years ago in the city of Prince Rupert. I am not criticizing the government because of the way they picked out their sites. I am advocating the establishment of a federal building in Prince Rupert, whether a site owned by the federal government be chosen or otherwise; I am not particular about that so long as Prince Rupert and central British Columbia are recognized. To my mind it is vital to have a federal building in that, portion of British North America. I call it British North America instead of British Columbia, because as I say we are the second port on the Pacific coast, Vancouver being the first. Sometimes it has been said that British Columbia is in Vancouver, but I ajfii here to demonstrate that Vancouver is in \British Columbia. I would like the house to learn where British Columbia is. I would ask hon. members not to look for Vancouver but to look for British Columbia, and they will find that there is such a place as Prince Rupert. When we receive the report concerning the Peace River outlet which my hen. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals is going to give us, I hope hon. members will study it and realize our geographical position. British Columbia requires not only the port of Vancouver but another port in order to do justice to the development of British North America, and Prince Rupert is the second port.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says "hear, hear". He is a friend of mine. I realize what he has in mind, but I am not prepared to go into that now. Probably we will need three or four ports, because in that part of the country we have room for millions of people. I represent a constituency which is bigger in area than England, Ireland, Scotland and Belgium combined.
Mr. Brady told us that.

Well, it is all right if you know it. I venture to say that- most hon. members do not know, however, that there is room for 30,000,000 people in that part of the country, and we have plenty of resources to back them up. We have agriculture, fishing, mining and all the resources to be found on God's earth. They are all in there.
When the government is considering the erection of public buildings I feel they should give my constituency some consideration. I know, however, that my hon. friend has it in mind and will give it due consideration. We are not trying to force the minister; I have no criticism to offer. However, I just wish to draw his attention to the magnitude of the country I represent, and especially the territory of Prince Rupert. The government is paying something like $7,000 a year by way of rental for a building that is nothing more than a shack. Why not erect a proper building and apply that $7,000 towards interest on the capital invested and thus have something for your money? By doing that we would get somewhere. I hope the present government will consider that proposition. If they do not now see the necessity for this accommodation at Prince Rupert, I have no doubt that some time they will, because I cannot believe they will leave it to their successors.

Not seeing any appropriation
in this item for the constituency I have the honour to represent, I would like to direct a few words to the Minister of Public Works. I was glad the hon. member began at last to talk about British Columbia, because although I have heard the north, south, east, and west mentioned, this is the first time British Columbia has been under consideration. Some of us are too far away. Three thousand miles is a long journey, and it is about time the members from British Columbia raised their voices. I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to some figures I have before me. For the erection of public buildings, out of a vote of over $6,000,000

Supply-Public Works-B.C.
British Columbia gets only $81,000. Out of that amount $8,000 is a revote. Expenditures authorized by statute amount to $579,712, and British Columbia gets only $112,000. For miscellaneous items the total amount is $929,000, nearly a million dollars, and of that amount British Columbia gets nothing. The total amount for roads and bridges is $173,250; of that amount British Columbia gets nothing. For telegraph and telephone lines the total amount is $205,950; of that amount British Columbia gets $63,600. Then we come to the heading "mail subsidies." There is a great deal of talk about the development of our markets. Of late we have been turning to the east to build up our trade. One would think that in connection with mail subsidies British Columbia would receive a substantial amount. Well, the total figure under this heading is $1,052,220 and of that amount British Columbia receives only $266,400. The total amount for ocean and river service is $3,697,300, and of that British Columbia receives only $20,000. The total amount for the marine department is $4,602,933, but of that British Columbia does not get a cent. I agree with the minister that we have to cut our suit according to the cloth, but I am afraid that on the suit he makes for Canada British Columbia will be represented by the buttonholes.
It will not be as bad as that.

Our appropriation has been cut down very considerably. I agree with the minister that we should exercise economy, but for public buildings we are cut down from $203,000 to $81,000, which is out of proportion to the decreased appropriations for the other provinces. Out of a total vote of something like $22,422,782 British Columbia is going to get only $880,000 odd. Is it any wonder we rise in our places and protest? I have long been of the opinion that British Columbia has been neglected by the federal authorities, but this is the first opportunity 1 have had of expressing that opinion in this house. As long as this neglect continues I am going to raise my voice in protest. It seems to me that the nearer you are to Ottawa the more you get.
Talking about public buildings, we have a post office at New Westminster that was built I do not know how many years ago. Practically all the mail for the Fraser valley goes through that post office. I venture to say that if the provincial department of health had any jurisdiction over government buildings they would have closed this one up long ago in view of the disgraceful conditions under which the postal staff are working.
They would do the same thing in Prince Rupert.

I ask the minister to consider this matter very seriously. The post office is so congested that the men are working back to back. The building should be enlarged, and we have the land for the purpose. I understand that last year the necessary plans were prepared in the department.
Have not these conditions prevailed for some years past?

I am not responsible for what happened in years past. Although my predecessor raised his voice in protest, apparently he did not raise it loud enough. Not only are we getting too small an appropriation in relation to our population, but we are getting a great deal less than the amount collected in relation to the duties on exports and imports through the ports of British Columbia. At one port alone the amount of duties collected is the second largest in the Dominion. In case it is urged that British Columbia has only a small population and does not amount to anything, I desire to put these figures on record. The duties collected last year at Vancouver amounted to $14,000,000, according to the returns given by the Department of Trade and Commerce. This figure is exceeded only by Montreal. The port of Quebec-where so much money has been spent-collected duties to the amount of only $2,500,000 odd. There the value of the imports for consumption amounted to $17,000,000 odd and of exports upwards of $12,000,000, while at Vancouver the value of the imports for consumption amounted to over $79,000,000 and of exports over $127,000,000. I am not going to plead the case of Vancouver, for she is ably represented in this house, but I should like to see the needs of British Columbia, and particularly the riding of New Westminster, taken into consideration by my hon. friend.

I would remind my hon. friend that the appropriations for public works are not based upon the population of the different provinces; they cannot be. Regard must be had for many factors. If he will go back through the public accounts I think he will find in some years that the expenditures on public buildings in his province have been out of proportion to the population-the basis for which he is now contending. He has already spoken to me about an appropriation for New Westminster. In that locality we have been spending a good deal on the Fraser river, but his request will be carefully considered.

Supply-Public Works-B.C.

Even during the last regime the port was not discriminated against because it happened to be represented by a member in opposition to the then government, as a matter of fact the appropriation was increased. I should like to see that policy continued. What is the reason for making such a great reduction in the appropriation?
The appropriation for any locality, I may tell my hon. friend, is not reduced because of the character or political complexion of its representation in this house, and it never will be.
I am very glad to hear that.
Put up that declaration in every post office.

Does the minister contemplate any increased accommodation at the Vancouver post office? He is probably aware that that post office is used as the centre from which all the mail going north and to many of the interior parts of the province is transferred. The present accommodation is not sufficient. I understand that recommendations have been made to the department for the past two or three years that further accommodation is necessary. Further, I understand that these recommendations have been endorsed by the minister's departmental officers. I repeat, this increased accommodation is urgently required, and I should like to know if the minister contemplates taking the necessary steps to provide it in the very near future.

In reply to the hon. member for Burrard I may say that I am informed that the matter has been receiving consideration for the last eight or ten years. Undoubtedly increased accommodation is necessary. I understand that it would cost approximately 8350,000 to acquire a site and about 81,000.000 to erect a building-a heavy expenditure. The matter is receiving consideration, and as soon as circumstances warrant action will be taken.

I am more or less familiar with the figures mentioned by the minister, but I would point out to him that the rentals now being paid for the accommodation of the various Dominion government services in the city represent interest on a capital investment that would amply take care of all these requirements. I think the minister will find that an increase in the public buildings in Vancouver would be justified as a good investment from the standpoint of the government.
Again I wish to point out that these expenditures are not made from capital as such, but from revenue.

May I suggest to the minister that it might entail less cost to the Dominion government to transfer some of the many federal offices we hear of in Vancouver up into the interior of the province, where I think you would get the site a good deal cheaper and the buildings would be constructed for a good deal less than the figures mentioned 'by the minister, for Vancouver. I offer this suggestion for his consideration.

I am sure my hon.
friend's constituents will welcome his suggestion, but I doubt whether it would be welcomed in other parts of British Columbia. People from all over the world, from British Columbia in particular and especially from that portion of the interior of British Columbia represented by my hon. friend, like an excuse to come to Vancouver, even if it is only to see one of the government officials.

I might also say that we welcome the people of Vancouver in the central part of British Columbia. It will not hurt the health of my hon. friend a bit to come into that part of the province and look at it once in a while.

When we go into that
part of the province its beauties are so great that we do not like to have our minds distracted by business.

Item agreed to.
Vancouver postal station "D"-improvements,
I would like the minister to explain this item.

This station is
in my hon. friend's constituency, I believe, and this amount is to provide for the installation of a new screen in postal station D for the purpose of providing improved postal facilities. The estimated cost is 81,800, with 8200 for contingencies.

Item agreed to.
Vancouver public building-to meet one year's interest at five per cent on mortgage of $400,000, $20,000.

Before we leave this
resolution I should like the minister to give the details of the appropriations which were not required for the last year.

Supply-Public Works

The appropriation for British Columbia was $128,300, and the expenditure was $112,879. The balance falls in, and I can give the hon. gentleman the particulars if he wishes them. For Vancouver public buildings, improvements and repairs, we voted $17,000 and only spent $14,995. For accommodation for the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve we voted SI 1,590 and spent $11,410, and the work is completed. For a public building in Trail $66,000 was appropriated and $56,648.46 was spent, and the building is completed. The balance falls in. For a public building at Rossland $5,000 was appropriated, S4.625.36 was spent and the building is completed. For a public building in Kimberley, $28,800 was appropriated; $25,195.28 was required for the construction of the building, and the balance falls in.
I should like as full information as I can get from the minister with regard to that appropriation for the R.C.N.V.R. accommodation.
Of last year?
Yes.

I am sorry I
have not the particulars of last year's appropriations with me.
I understand that appropriation was made for the purpose of acquiring the old buildings of the Royal Vancouver Yacht Club.
That is correct.

That item went through last year. I understand a cheque has been issued so that it will come out of last year's estimates, but as yet the cheque has not been sent out. The point I wish to make is this: The government rented that property from the yacht club and paid a rental of $1,800 a year. They had the opportunity of purchasing the property at $10,000, I think, and they considered that expenditure justified. However, it is now over a year since the appropriation was made and I understand that the yacht club have received neither cheque nor rental in the meantime. I think they are at least entitled to receive rental, and failing that I think they should receive interest for the time the payment has been held up.

I assure my hon. friend that this matter will be brought to the
attention of departmental officials. The matter will be checked up, and if there are any errors they will be corrected.

Just for the information of the minister I might say that I understand the papers in that connection are in the possession of the Department of Justice now and are being held up there because the department is anxious to secure a right of way to this property from the city of Vancouver. However, the sale of the property did not contemplate that the club would be required to give this right of way, which is in the control of the city of Vancouver. That is the cause of the delay, and I do not think there is any justification for withholding that payment.
Could the minister give us some information with regard to this interest of five per cent on the mortgage of $400,000?
It was the Winch building, which was purchased by the former government subject to a mortgage, and we. are paying the interest on the mortgage.

Item agreed to.
Public buildings generally - experimental farms-replacements, repairs, improvements, etc., $50,000.

Having regard to the fact that the announced policy of this government is that it will take a strong forward movement on behalf of agriculture, this cut from $100,000 to $50,000 is rather an unhappy exemplification of that strong attitude. Especially is that so when I find the Prime Minister reported in the Telegraph-Journal of St. John, under date of July 3, as saying that he would regard it as a great responsibility, if elected, to see that the collective weight and power of the Dominion is placed behind agriculture. I think this is rather an unfortunate illustration of that power, to cut down this item from $100,000 to $50,000. I suppose this will include new buildings as well?
No, this is just for ordinary repairs.

It is the regular vote, but the amount is irregularly small. It covers some twenty-five farms, including the tobacco farms, and I feel sure that the Minister of Agriculture, who is present, could very well use that other $50,000 to keep those farms in good order during the coming year.
Supply-Public Works

Sometimes it is easier to get through two small bites than one large bite; that often has been found to be the case in the past, and I would suggest that a second bite be taken in the supplementary estimates. I am sure it would be a welcome contribution to the system of experimental farms so well kept up for the last eight or ten years.
What amount was expended last year?	.

While the information requested by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough is being looked up, I can only say to the hon. member for Melville that this reduction will not curtail the extension of any agricultural program which may be adopted. This is just to cover minor, casual repairs and improvements that come along from time to time. We think we can get through this year with that amount.
It is a bad start
I am sorry, but the officer informs me that he has not the information as to the amount spent last year. However, we can get it.

Item agreed to.
Public buildings generally-military buildings -repairs, fittings and additions, $50,000.

In connection with
military buildings, I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the condition in Vancouver. He is probably quite familiar with the situation. I do not propose to criticize the expenditure he is making this year in connection with the rental of the horse show building, which is now used there, but it seems to me that the rental being paid is exorbitant. It cannot be avoided at the present time, but I do think it is very necessary for the government to consider the whole situation in regard to militia units in Vancouver. The government are paying $9,000 at present for the horse show building, and I am informed that the purchase price of that building was approximately $25,000 to $27,000. There is no other building in Vancouver at present suitable. Now, housed in that building are military stores to the value of between $400,000 and $500,000. The place is nothing but a fire trap, and if the government are going to continue militia establishments at all they would most certainly be well advised to consider seriously the building of an armoury, to capitalize the sum that is paid now and to obviate the risk to this military equipment. I would suggest that the minister give that serious consideration. At present we have there other military units

that are improperly housed. Under the present system of renting quarters it is practically impossible for them to better their condition, and again I suggest that if we are to continue militia units the government should consider some accommodation that would justify the efforts of these officers and men and the time they are putting in. We should give them quarters much more suitable than those they have at present.

This lease has
been current for some years. I thank the hon. gentleman for his information, which will be taken into consideration. I should like to pass this item to-night, if possible.

I wish to refer very briefly
to the Shaughnessy hospital, which is in bad condition. It is a fire trap. I took the matter up with the Minister of Pensions and National Health and he indicated that there had been an attempt to reduce the fire risk by placing in another building some of the worst cases in the upper stories, and including in the estimates a substantial sum for rebuilding or repairing the place. Is there any vote for the Shaughnessy hospital concealed in this estimate?
There is nothing in this estimate to cover the item to which the hon. member refers.
But this is for military buildings-repairs.

That is only
repairs.

Well, this building should be repaired; something should be done to it. It is really in a dangerous condition now. As I say, it is a fire trap. My hon. friend (Mr. Hanbury) is quite right when he refers to another building as being a fire trap for military stores. But surely where human life is concerned, the matter is much more serious.

I wish
to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni with reference to the Shaughnessy hospital. I would impress upon the Minister of Pensions and, as well, upon the Minister of Public Works the necessity for a new military hospital in Vancouver. I think my recollection is correct, that the previous administration had prepared plans for a new military7 hospital there, and I wish to urge upon this government the importance of this undertaking.
